recipe: T extends U ? X : Y distributes over unions only when T is a naked type parameter. Wrap both sides — [T] extends [U] — to compare the union as one whole type.
Distribution is per-member instantiation, then union. ToArray<string|number> is string[]|number[]; the bracketed form gives (string|number)[]. Pick deliberately, it is not a style choice.
never is the empty union, so a distributive conditional over it produces never, not the true branch. F<never> is never even though never extends never is true.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript issue #31751 (conditional type with never argument)

recipe: To actually test for never, disable distribution: [T] extends [never] ? yes : no. The naked form silently returns never and is a classic wrong-but-confident answer.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript issue #23182 (extends never only works sometimes)

recipe: boolean is true | false, so a naked distributive conditional splits it and you get a union of both branches. Bracket the check when you mean boolean as one type.
infer declares a type variable inside the extends clause and may only be referenced in the true branch. Element of an array: T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? U : never.
Multiple infer sites for one variable: candidates from covariant positions union, candidates from contravariant positions intersect. {a:(x:infer U)=>void, b:(x:infer U)=>void} yields string & number.
infer S extends string (4.7) folds the nested check into the match: if S is not a string the conditional takes the false branch, replacing an inner S extends string ? S : never.
infer is illegal in a type parameter constraint. type R<T extends (...a:any[]) => infer X> = X does not compile; move the infer into a conditional in the body.
Match any callable with (...args: never[]) => infer R rather than any[]. never[] is the bottom parameter list, so contravariance makes it accept the widest set of signatures.
Conditional types may reference themselves inside their branches since 4.1. Awaited<T> = T extends PromiseLike<infer U> ? Awaited<U> : T is the canonical shape.
Tuple recursion: T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? ... : ... . Variadic tuple spreads and non-final rest elements, both 4.0, are what make head/tail walking possible.
Exclude<T,U> = T extends U ? never : T and Extract<T,U> = T extends U ? T : never are nothing but distribution wrappers. On a non-naked or bracketed T they do nothing useful.
NonNullable<T> is now T & {}, not a conditional (4.8). Intersections reduce and are assignable to, so NonNullable<NonNullable<T>> simplifies where the conditional form stayed deferred forever.
unknown is exactly {} | null | undefined since 4.8, which is why T & {} works as NonNullable and why truthiness-narrowing an unknown now gives you {}.
Inside a generic, a conditional on an unresolved T stays deferred. 5.4 stopped using the constraint to choose a branch, so you get a union and neither branch is assignable.
{ [P in keyof T]: X } is homomorphic and preserves T's readonly and ? modifiers by default. That preservation is why Partial and Readonly compose instead of flattening.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #21919 (improved control over mapped type modifiers)

recipe: Homomorphism needs the literal keyof T form. Hoisting the keys into an alias first (K = keyof T; { [P in K]: T[P] }) makes it non-homomorphic and silently drops modifiers.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #21919 (improved control over mapped type modifiers)

recipe: A homomorphic mapped type over a tuple or array produces a tuple or array, not an object with push and length mapped. MapToPromise<[number,number]> is [Promise<number>,Promise<number>].
+readonly/-readonly and +?/-? add or remove modifiers; a bare modifier means +. Under strictNullChecks, -? also strips undefined from the property type, which is how Required works.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #21919 (improved control over mapped type modifiers)

recipe: Readonly<T> maps an array to readonly T[] and a tuple to a readonly tuple since 3.4. Earlier it mapped Array's own members and produced nonsense.
as clauses rename keys (4.1): [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]. The & string is mandatory because keyof T also contains number and symbol.
Produce never in the as clause to drop a key: [K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? K : never]. Replaces Omit plus a key-collecting helper.
Map over a union of objects using a discriminant as the key: { [E in Events as E['kind']]: (e: E) => void }. The union members, not keyof, drive the key set.
Pick and Omit do not distribute. Omit<A|B,'k'> collapses to the shared properties and destroys narrowing. Wrap it: T extends unknown ? Omit<T,K> : never, as type-fest's DistributedOmit does.
Except-style helpers only allow omitting keys present in every union member; a distributed version allows keys present in any member. Different constraints, different call sites break.
keyof over a string index signature is string | number, not string, because JS coerces numeric keys to strings. A number index signature gives just number.
Index signatures take template patterns and symbol since 4.4: [k: `data-${string}`]: unknown. [k: string | symbol] desugars into two separate signatures.
A conditional in the value position transforms per property; a conditional in the as clause filters keys. Same syntax, completely different output shape — do not mix them up.
Know the shapes rather than importing: Partial { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] }, Required { [P in keyof T]-?: T[P] }, Readonly { readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P] }.
exactOptionalPropertyTypes (4.4) makes age?: number reject an explicit undefined. Mapped types that add ? then no longer smuggle undefined into the value type.
Every union in an interpolation slot cross-multiplies. `${V}-${H}` with three each is nine members; add a third slot and you are multiplying, not adding.
The union cap is about 100,000 members. Empirically at 4.5.4, `${Range<0,316>}-${Range<0,316>}` compiles and one more step gives TS2590, too complex to represent.
source_name: francium.cc: The limits of TypeScript's Template Literal types

recipe: Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize and Uncapitalize are compiler intrinsics (4.1) backed by JS toUpperCase/toLowerCase. They are not locale-aware; do not use them for user-facing text.
Split a string type with infer in the literal: S extends `${infer H}${infer R}`. Matching is leftmost; anchor with literal separators when you want a specific boundary.
`${infer N extends number}` (4.8) yields the literal 100, not number. Conversion must round-trip: '1.0' falls back to number because String(Number('1.0')) is '1'.
Same trick for bigint and boolean: '100' with infer U extends bigint gives 100n, 'true' with infer U extends boolean gives true. Without the constraint you only get the base primitive.
TypeScript 7.0 infers on Unicode code points, not UTF-16 units. HeadTail<'😀abc'> is now ['😀','abc'] where it used to return surrogate halves. A real behaviour break for string parsers.
Template literals are safe when the alphabet stays open and dangerous when you enumerate it. The handbook itself says generate large string unions ahead of time instead.
To constrain keys without enumerating them, use a pattern index signature: [k: `data-${string}`]: unknown. Cheap where the equivalent union would explode.
Trim<S> = S extends ` ${infer T}` ? Trim<T> : S extends `${infer T} ` ? Trim<T> : S. Tail position, so it loops to 1000 instead of dying at the depth limit.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #45711 (tail recursive evaluation of conditional types)

recipe: Bounded key patterns are the sweet spot: on<K extends string & keyof T>(e: `${K}Changed`, cb: (v: T[K]) => void). The union is already capped by keyof T.
5.4 made checking strings against template placeholders more accurate: inside a generic, `-${keyof T & string}` now accepts '-id' where it used to error.
strictFunctionTypes makes function-typed parameters contravariant — but only for function syntax. Method syntax stays bivariant, deliberately, and the flag does not touch it.
{ func(x: string|number): void } happily accepts (x: string) => void, and m.func(10) is never flagged. Unsound, documented, and unchanged by any strict flag.
Method bivariance is load-bearing, not an oversight: enforcing contravariance breaks array covariance and a large number of existing hierarchies, including parts of the DOM.
Three documented unsound assignabilities: Dog[] to Animal[], fewer-parameter functions where more are expected, and non-void returns to void-returning callbacks. All three are relied on daily.
Array covariance is the one that bites: the target can be written through. Take readonly T[] in any signature that only reads, and the variance becomes sound.
in, out and in out (4.7) declare contravariant, covariant and invariant type parameters. They are checked against usage — declaring out while using T in an input position errors.
You may declare stricter than reality: marking a covariant parameter in out is accepted with no complaint. The annotation is a claim TypeScript will honour, not always verify.
Their real job is short-circuiting variance computation on circular or deeply recursive generics. Library-author tool, not something to sprinkle on every type parameter.
Excess property checking only fires on fresh object literals. Assign through an intermediate const and it vanishes, because object types are not sealed and a value may carry extra members.
Against a union, a property is excess only if it belongs to no constituent. A literal that pins one discriminant can still carry another member's properties uncaught — a known design limitation.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript issue #35890 (no excess property check for discriminated union)

recipe: satisfies re-arms excess property checking on a literal while keeping the narrow inferred type: the 'bleu' typo errors and palette.green still has string methods.
Classes are structural except for private and protected members, which must originate in the same declaration to be considered the same member. That is the only built-in nominality.
No nominal types, so brand with an intersection carrying a phantom property: type Url = string & { readonly [tag]: 'Url' }. Cost is a cast at every construction site.
A branded type is assignable to its base, never the reverse. The base is not hidden, so a brand is a one-way gate, not an opaque type — and it vanishes at runtime.
3.9 checks every member of an intersection against the target. A & B assignable to C now fails when A's a: number clashes with C's a?: boolean; before, matching B was enough.
Three different tools: an annotation checks and replaces the type, as asserts without checking, satisfies checks and keeps the inferred type. Reach for satisfies on config objects.
Record<Colors, string|RGB> as an annotation makes every value string|RGB. The same type after satisfies keeps red as a tuple and green as a string. That is the whole point.
<const T> (5.0) infers as though the caller wrote as const, but only for literals written at the call site. Pass a pre-computed const arr and you still get string[].
<const T extends string[]> silently falls back to string[], because readonly ['a','b'] is not assignable to a mutable array. Always write extends readonly string[].
NoInfer<T> (5.4) stops a position contributing inference candidates. (colors: C[], def?: NoInfer<C>) makes a stray 'blue' an error instead of widening C to include it.
as const does three things: no literal widening, readonly properties, readonly tuples. It applies only to literal expressions — (60*60*1000) as const is an error.
as const is not a deep freeze. A referenced array keeps its own mutability: foo.contents = [] errors, foo.contents.push(5) compiles fine.
3.4 propagates free type parameters through generic function arguments, so compose(makeArray, makeBox) is <T>(arg: T) => Box<T[]> instead of collapsing to {}.
When you need literal inference and cannot change the callee, route through a generic identity helper: const asTuple = <const T>(x: T) => x. The type parameter is what makes inference fire.
5.5 infers x is T when a function has no return annotation, exactly one return statement, never mutates the parameter, and returns an expression that refines it.
Truthiness blocks inference: .filter(s => !!s) gets no predicate — and would silently drop 0. .filter(s => s !== undefined) gets one. Prefer explicit comparisons.
5.5 narrows existing code: [1,2,null].filter(x => x !== null) is now number[], so a later push(null) errors. Annotate the receiving variable to opt back out.
5.8 checks each branch of a conditional expression in a return against the declared return type separately, so an any branch no longer swallows a wrong sibling branch.
5.9 tightened leaks of type variables during inference. New errors appear in generic-heavy call sites and are usually fixed by passing type arguments explicitly.
Contextual typing is what keeps literals narrow inside a call; nothing keeps them narrow across a let. const gets the literal, let gets the widened type.
A discriminant must be a literal type. kind: string does not narrow; kind: 'circle' does. Define each member as its own interface and union them.
Exhaustiveness: default: { const _x: never = shape; return _x; }. Adding a union member breaks that assignment at compile time, which is the only reliable alarm.
never is assignable to every type and nothing but never is assignable to never. That asymmetry is the entire mechanism behind exhaustiveness checks.
4.4 narrows through an aliased condition and a destructured discriminant, but only when the alias is const or readonly and the source is never reassigned.
4.6 narrows dependent parameters only when the signature is a rest tuple union: (...args: ['a', number] | ['b', string]). Two independent parameters will never co-narrow.
5.4 preserves narrowing inside a closure created after the last assignment. Any assignment to that variable from inside any nested function kills the refinement again.
typeof null is 'object', so typeof x === 'object' leaves string[] | null still nullable. Check null explicitly rather than trusting the typeof branch.
The in operator narrows by property presence, but an optional property leaves the type present in both branches. Useless as a discriminant when the key is optional.
arg is T predicates are unchecked: the body can lie and the compiler believes it. They are assertions with pleasant syntax, not proofs — treat them as trusted boundaries.
asserts cond and asserts val is T (3.7) narrow for the remainder of the scope. Call sites require the callee declared with an explicit type annotation, or you get TS2775.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript issue #34523 (asserts x is T with arrow functions)

recipe: Since 3.9 an intersection with conflicting discriminants collapses the whole type to never, not just the clashing member: (Circle & Square).kind errors on never.
5.4 reduces intersections against constraints: with T extends 'abc'|'def', T & string is now T and T & number is never. Intersections with type variables are no longer inert.
Force distribution over a union with T extends unknown ? F<T> : never. That single wrapper is how you make any non-distributive utility act per member.
5.0 made every enum a union enum, giving computed members unique types so they narrow. It also made let m: SomeEvenDigit = 1 an error.
useUnknownInCatchVariables (4.4) types catch variables unknown. Narrow with instanceof Error before touching .message rather than annotating err: any.
'Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite' means the instantiation depth limit was crossed. That limit is 100, lowered from 500 when tail recursion landed.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #45711 (tail recursive evaluation of conditional types)

recipe: The 1000-iteration budget applies only to conditionals resolved in the loop, not to types that recurse through a union or a tuple construction in a non-tail position.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #45711 (tail recursive evaluation of conditional types)

recipe: TS2590, 'Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent', is a different limit from depth: roughly 100,000 union members. Splitting recursion depth will not fix it.
source_name: francium.cc: The limits of TypeScript's Template Literal types

recipe: Empirically at 4.5.4: Range<0,999> compiles, Range<0,1000> hits the depth error. Numeric ranges above about a thousand do not belong in the type system.
source_name: francium.cc: The limits of TypeScript's Template Literal types

recipe: 4.6 separated explicitly written deep nesting from depth generated while exploring. Foo<Foo<Foo<Foo<Foo<Foo<string>>>>>> = Foo<...five...> now correctly errors where it used to be accepted.
5.9 caches intermediate instantiations on mappers, which removed spurious excessive-depth errors in Zod- and tRPC-shaped libraries. Sometimes upgrading the compiler is the entire fix.

Inside f<T>(x: T): IsArray<T>, neither true nor false is assignable to the deferred conditional — both error. Correct programs are rejected; an overload or a cast at the boundary is the accepted escape.
Branding costs interop: a cast at every construction site, no structural round-trip through JSON, and a phantom property that exists only in the type system.
The 4.1 notes are blunt about type-level computation: better not to use these types at all than to ship one that fails on realistic inputs. Do not put a Fibonacci type in a published .d.ts.
Types are erased. For JSON, network payloads or user input, validate at runtime and carry the result into the type system with a predicate or an assertion function.
TypeScript 7.0 (July 2026) is a Go port, not a redesign: code compiling cleanly on 6.0 should compile identically. The one type-level break is Unicode-aware template literal inference.
Prefer a lookup over computation where possible: an indexed access T[K] or a mapped record costs nothing, while the equivalent recursive conditional burns depth budget.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #45711 (tail recursive evaluation of conditional types)

recipe: @ts-expect-error (3.9) suppresses the next line and errors when there was nothing to suppress: 'Unused @ts-expect-error directive'. @ts-ignore is silent either way, so only the former is a test.
Canonical strict equality: type Equal<X,Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false. It leans on internal identity of deferred conditionals.
type-challenges' assertion pair is Expect<T extends true> and ExpectFalse<T extends false>, used as type cases = [Expect<Equal<Actual, Expected>>]. No runtime, no dependencies.
IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false. Test for it, because any passes and fails every extends check and quietly makes a whole assertion suite vacuously true.
expectTypeOf(x).toEqualTypeOf<T>() is exact equality, .toExtend<T>() is assignability, .toBeNumber() allows subtypes. Types only — no CLI and no build step.
.branded rewrites both sides into a pseudo-AST so {a:1}&{b:2} compares equal to {a:1;b:2}. Expensive; use it only when toEqualTypeOf fails on structurally identical intersections.
.branded.inspect() finds an any, never or unknown buried deep in a nested type — usually the reason a type test passes when it should not.

expect-type treats overloads as a union of all variants, capped at ten, rather than following Parameters/ReturnType which only see the last signature. Stricter, and occasionally the difference that matters.

tsd: expectType<T> is identical-type, expectAssignable/expectNotAssignable are looser, expectError asserts the expression errors, expectNever asserts never, printType prints the computed type. MIT, runs as a CLI.
tsd's expectError does not ignore syntax errors, so a malformed expression still fails rather than passing as 'it errored'. Useful, but @ts-expect-error pins the error to one line.
dtslint's $ExpectType and $ExpectError plus '// Minimum TypeScript Version: x.y' is the DefinitelyTyped convention. The standalone repo is archived; it now ships as @definitelytyped/dtslint.
The dtslint README itself says: just looking for ExpectType and ExpectError? Use tsd. Reserve dtslint for DefinitelyTyped-style multi-version matrices.
A type test suite without negative cases only proves everything is any. Assert both that the good input compiles and that the bad input is rejected.
Type-level behaviour is version-sensitive — distribution, infer extends, NoInfer, inferred predicates. Pin and test across every TypeScript version you claim to support, as DefinitelyTyped does.
